meta.name: engram bake-off test set v1
meta.purpose: Gate the next-step decision: compare (a) frontier model + search, (b) engram, (c) PaperQA2 on the same corpus with current models. Scored on retrieval correctness + citation support + answer correctness.
meta.corpus_caveat: 5 famous ML/RAG papers a frontier model likely already knows; questions deliberately target specific, hard-to-memorize details (exact numbers, table cells, ablations). Swap in private/biomedical papers later for the 'do we need a corpus?' verdict.

papers.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
Leveraging Passage Retrieval with Generative Models for Open Domain Question Answering (Fusion-in-Decoder)
HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models
LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation

questions.question: In the base Transformer, what are the values of the number of attention heads (h) and the per-head key/value dimensions (d_k and d_v), and how is d_k derived from d_model?
questions.answer: h = 8 heads, with d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 64.
questions.supporting_quote: In this work we employ h = 8 parallel attention layers, or heads. For each of these we use dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64.

questions.question: What Adam optimizer hyperparameters (beta1, beta2, epsilon) and warmup_steps value were used to train the Transformer?
questions.answer: Adam with beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.98, epsilon = 10^-9, and warmup_steps = 4000.
questions.supporting_quote: We used the Adam optimizer with beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.98 and epsilon = 10-9. ... We used warmup_steps = 4000.

questions.question: On the WMT 2014 English-to-French task, what BLEU score did the big Transformer achieve, and what dropout rate P_drop was used for that English-to-French big model (as opposed to the English-to-German big model)?
questions.answer: BLEU of 41.8, using dropout P_drop = 0.1 (instead of 0.3).
questions.supporting_quote: The Transformer (big) model trained for English-to-French used dropout rate Pdrop = 0.1, instead of 0.3.

questions.question: In the Table 3 ablations (rows A), how much worse in BLEU is single-head attention compared to the best head setting?
questions.answer: Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting.
questions.supporting_quote: While single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, quality also drops off with too many heads.

questions.question: What hardware was used to train the models, and how many training steps and how much wall-clock time did the base model versus the big model take?
questions.answer: 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs; the base model trained for 100,000 steps (12 hours, ~0.4 s/step) and the big model for 300,000 steps (3.5 days, ~1.0 s/step).
questions.supporting_quote: We trained our models on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. ... We trained the base models for a total of 100,000 steps or 12 hours. ... The big models were trained for 300,000 steps (3.5 days).

questions.question: In BERT's masked LM pre-training, the data generator selects 15% of token positions for prediction. Of those selected tokens, what are the three replacement probabilities and what does each replace the token with?
questions.answer: 80% of the time replaced with the [MASK] token, 10% of the time with a random token, and 10% of the time left unchanged.
questions.supporting_quote: we replace the i-th word with (1) the [MASK] token 80% of the time (2) a random token 10% of the time (3) the unchanged i-th word 10% of the time.

questions.question: On the official GLUE leaderboard reported in the paper, what score does BERT_LARGE obtain, and what score does OpenAI GPT obtain as of the date of writing?
questions.answer: BERT_LARGE obtains 80.5; OpenAI GPT obtains 72.8.
questions.supporting_quote: On the official GLUE leaderboard, BERT_LARGE obtains a score of 80.5, compared to OpenAI GPT, which obtains 72.8 as of the date of writing.

questions.question: In the model-size ablation (Table 6), what is the masked LM perplexity on held-out data for the smallest model (L=3, H=768, A=12) versus the largest model (L=24, H=1024, A=16)?
questions.answer: The smallest model (L=3) has LM perplexity 5.84; the largest model (L=24) has LM perplexity 3.23.

questions.question: What optimizer and hyperparameters (learning rate, beta1, beta2, L2 weight decay) were used to pre-train BERT, and what was the learning-rate warmup schedule?
questions.answer: Adam, learning rate 1e-4, beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.999, L2 weight decay 0.01, warmup over the first 10,000 steps then linear decay.
questions.supporting_quote: We use Adam with learning rate of 1e-4, beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.999, L2 weight decay of 0.01, learning rate warmup over the first 10,000 steps, and linear decay of the learning rate.

questions.question: What accuracy does the final BERT model achieve on the Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task?
questions.answer: 97%-98% accuracy on NSP.
questions.supporting_quote: The final model achieves 97%-98% accuracy on NSP.

questions.question: In the Fusion-in-Decoder reading model, which three special tokens are added before the question, title, and text of each passage when constructing the encoder input?
questions.answer: question:, title:, and context:
questions.supporting_quote: We add special tokens question:, title: and context: before the question, title and text of each passage.

questions.question: In Table 1, what exact-match (EM) score does Fusion-in-Decoder (large) achieve on the NaturalQuestions test set, and how does it compare to the base model?
questions.answer: 51.4 EM for the large model versus 48.2 EM for the base model.
questions.supporting_quote: Fusion-in-Decoder (base) 48.2 ... Fusion-in-Decoder (large) 51.4

questions.question: What were the two model sizes (base and large) in parameters, and what optimizer, constant learning rate, dropout rate, number of gradient steps, and batch size were used for fine-tuning?
questions.answer: Base = 220M, large = 770M; Adam with constant learning rate 10^-4, 10% dropout, 10k gradient steps, batch size 64, on 64 Tesla V100 32Gb.
questions.supporting_quote: We consider two model sizes, base and large, containing respectively 220M and 770M parameters. ... using Adam with a constant learning rate of 10^-4 and a dropout rate of 10%. We train the model for 10k gradient steps, with a batch size of 64, using 64 Tesla V100 32Gb.

questions.question: When fine-tuning a model previously trained on fewer passages (finetuning with 100 passages for 1000 steps), what NaturalQuestions EM does it reach and how many GPU hours does it cost compared to training on 100 passages from the start?
questions.answer: 46.0 EM on NaturalQuestions using 147 GPU hours, versus 425 GPU hours when training on 100 passages from scratch.
questions.supporting_quote: we can reach 46.0 EM on NaturalQuestions, using 147 GPU hours, compared to 425 GPU hours when training on 100 passages.
questions.section: 4 Experiments (Impact of number of training passages)

questions.question: In Table 2, what NaturalQuestions dev EM does the model obtain when trained with 5 passages without finetuning, and what does it become with finetuning?
questions.answer: 37.8 EM without finetuning and 45.0 EM with finetuning (at 5 training passages).

questions.question: In HippoRAG's implementation details, what values are used for the synonymy threshold (tau) and the PPR damping factor, and how many MuSiQue training examples were used to tune them?
questions.answer: Synonymy threshold tau = 0.8, PPR damping factor = 0.5, tuned using 100 examples from MuSiQue's training data.
questions.supporting_quote: We use 100 examples from MuSiQue's training data to tune HippoRAG's two hyperparameters: the synonymy threshold tau at 0.8 and the PPR damping factor at 0.5

questions.question: According to the retrieval corpora statistics in Table 1, how many unique nodes (N) and unique edges (E) were extracted for the MuSiQue dataset?
questions.answer: 91,729 unique nodes and 21,714 unique edges.
questions.supporting_quote: # of Unique Nodes (N) ... 91,729 ... # of Unique Edges (E) ... 21,714

questions.question: In the single-step retrieval results (Table 2), what R@2 and R@5 scores did HippoRAG (Contriever) achieve on the 2WikiMultiHopQA dataset?
questions.supporting_quote: HippoRAG (Contriever) ... 71.5 89.5

questions.question: In the 'Dissecting HippoRAG' ablation (Table 5), when HippoRAG's OpenIE module is replaced with the end-to-end model REBEL, what is the average R@2 across the three datasets, and how does it compare to the full HippoRAG average R@2?
questions.answer: REBEL achieves an average R@2 of 46.2, versus 57.4 for full HippoRAG (a drop of 11.2 points).

questions.question: Using the all-recall (AR) metric in Table 6, what AR@2 scores did ColBERTv2 and HippoRAG achieve on 2WikiMultiHopQA (the percentage of queries for which all supporting passages are retrieved)?
questions.answer: ColBERTv2 achieved AR@2 = 25.1 and HippoRAG achieved AR@2 = 45.4 on 2Wiki.

questions.question: In LightRAG's experimental setup, what chunk size and gleaning parameter values were used across all datasets, and which LLM was the default for all LLM-based operations?
questions.answer: Chunk size = 1200, gleaning parameter = 1 (for both GraphRAG and LightRAG), default LLM = GPT-4o-mini.
questions.supporting_quote: For all LLM-based operations in LightRAG, we default to using GPT-4o-mini. To ensure consistency, the chunk size is set to 1200 across all datasets. Additionally, the gleaning parameter is fixed at 1 for both GraphRAG and LightRAG.

questions.question: According to Table 4, how many documents and total tokens does the Legal dataset (the largest of the four UltraDomain datasets) contain?
questions.answer: 94 documents and 5,081,069 total tokens.
questions.supporting_quote: The Legal dataset is the largest, comprising 94 documents and 5,081,069 tokens.

questions.question: In the win-rate comparison (Table 1) on the Legal dataset, what Overall win rate did LightRAG achieve against the GraphRAG baseline?
questions.answer: 52.8% (versus GraphRAG's 47.2%).
questions.supporting_quote: Overall 47.2% 52.8%

questions.question: In the ablation study (Table 2), what does the '-Origin' variant remove, and what was its observed effect on performance?
questions.answer: It eliminates the use of original text in retrieval; it did not cause significant declines and in some cases (Agriculture, Mix) even improved performance.
questions.supporting_quote: We eliminated the use of original text in our retrieval process. Surprisingly, the resulting variant, -Origin, does not exhibit significant performance declines across all four datasets. In some cases, this variant even shows improvements (e.g. in Agriculture and Mix).

questions.question: In the cost analysis on the Legal dataset, how many communities did GraphRAG generate, how many level-2 communities were actively used for retrieval, and what is the approximate token cost per community report during incremental updates?
questions.answer: 1,399 communities, 610 level-2 communities used for retrieval, ~5,000 tokens per community report.
questions.supporting_quote: GraphRAG generates 1,399 communities, with 610 level-2 communities actively utilized for retrieval in this experiment... approximately 5,000 tokens per community report.
